When the primary vessels govern the illness, there is harmony. 

When the illness is contracted within the sinews and bone marrow, and the pulse is intermittent while also surging, the illness is contracted from wine and sexual indulgence. The reason one knows that after five days an ulcerated swelling would form, and after eight days he would vomit pus and die, is that when examining his pulse, the lesser <term>yang</term> <gloss>active, exterior bodily principle</gloss> had begun to alternate. An alternating pulse indicates a disease of the primary vessel. When the illness passes, it moves to the human body; entering the human body, it moves into the collateral vessels governing the illness. At that time, the lesser yang pulse had first reached one tenth of an inch at the barrier position. Therefore, there was internal heat, but the pus had not yet erupted. When it reached five tenths of an inch, it reached the boundary of the lesser yang. 

<note>Collected Explanations: Xu Guang says: 'One' is also written as 'tenth'. The later chapter states that the liver and heart are five tenths of an inch apart, which is why it is said that after five days it is exhausted.</note> <note>Correct Meaning: Wang Shuhe's Pulse Classic states: 'Distinguishing the boundaries of the three gates and what the pulse signs govern: It is said that from the fish border to the high bone, moving backward one inch, the middle is called the cun mouth. From the high bone past the cun to the cubit, it is called the cubit marsh. Therefore it is called cun and cubit. Behind the cubit and in front of the cun is called the barrier. Yang emerges and yin enters, with the barrier serving as the boundary. Yang emerges three tenths of an inch, hence it is called three yin and three yang. Yang is born at the cubit and moves at the cun. Yin is born at the cun and moves at the cubit. The cun governs directing upward to the upper burner, emerging at the head and skin and hair, reaching the hands.'</note>

The <term>liver</term> <gloss>gan</gloss> weighs four catties and four ounces. It has three lobes on the left and four lobes on the right, making seven lobes in total. It governs the storing of the <term>ethereal soul</term> <gloss>hun</gloss>. The liver is a trunk <note>original: "幹", a pun on gan</note>. In the Five Elements, it is Wood, and its physical form has branches and trunks. Another source says that the liver spirits are six boys and three girls. 

The <term>heart</term> <gloss>xin</gloss> weighs twelve ounces. Within it are seven pores and three hairs. It contains three tenths of a pint of seminal fluid. It governs the storing of the <term>spirit</term> <gloss>shen</gloss>. The heart is fine and subtle <note>original: "纖", a pun on xin</note>, for what it perceives is subtle and delicate. Its spirit is Nine Grand Commanders <note>original: "九太尉公"</note>, named Grand Origin of the Crimson Palace, Venerable Person of the South Pole <note>original: "絳宮太始南極老人"</note>, possessing a body of circular radiance, with three thousand six hundred attendant officials. It is also the sovereign ruler of the body. 

The <term>spleen</term> <gloss>pi</gloss> weighs two catties and three ounces. It is flat and three inches wide, five inches long, and has half a catty of diffuse fatty tissue. It governs the wrapping of blood and warming of the five <term>viscera</term> <gloss>zang</gloss>, and governs the storing of <term>intention</term> <gloss>yi</gloss>. The spleen provides assistance <note>original: "裨", a pun on pi</note>, aiding the vital energy and governing the transformation of grain. Its spirit is called the Jade Maiden Mother of Radiant Cloud <note>original: "雲光玉女子母"</note>, with three thousand six hundred attendant officials. 

The <term>lungs</term> <gloss>fei</gloss> weigh three catties and three ounces. They have six lobes and two ears, making eight lobes in total. They govern the storing of the ethereal soul and corporeal soul <note>original: "魂魄"</note>. The lungs mean sudden flourish <note>original: "孛", a pun on fei</note>, meaning that their vital energy flourishes suddenly and is therefore short, being congested. Their spirit is eight persons, the Lords of Great Harmony <note>original: "太和君"</note>, named Jade Hall Palace, Imperial Secretarial Bureau <note>original: "玉堂宮尚書府"</note>, with three thousand six hundred attendant officials. In the court discussion, he said, "Whenever Han has concluded a marriage alliance with the Xiongnu, it rarely lasted more than a few years before they broke the treaty again. It would be better not to grant it, but rather to raise troops and attack them."

Anguo said, "Fighting across a thousand leagues brings no advantage to an army. At present, the Xiongnu rely on the swiftness of their warhorses and harbor the hearts of beasts. Moving like birds taking flight, they are difficult to capture and control. Winning their lands is not enough to expand our territory; taking their populace is not enough to strengthen our state. Since high antiquity, they have never been reckoned as subjects of our civilization <note><term>Suoyin</term> <gloss>Seeking the Obscure</gloss>: Jin Zhuo states that they did not submit internally to Han to become civilized subjects.</note>. If Han marches several thousand leagues to vie for gain, men and horses will be exhausted, while the enemy will use their full strength to exploit our weariness. Furthermore, when an arrow shot from a powerful crossbow reaches the end of its flight, it cannot pierce even thin Lu silk <note><term>Jijie</term> <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss>: Xu Shen says that the silk of Lu was exceptionally thin.</note>; when a tempest dies down, its final force cannot stir a swan's down. This is not because the shot or the wind lacked vigor at first, but because their strength fades at the end. Launching an attack on them would be unfavorable. It is better to grant the marriage alliance."

Li Si and Yao Jia grew jealous of him and defamed him, saying: "Han Fei is a noble scion of the ducal house of Han. Now, Your Majesty wishes to annex all the feudal lords; Fei will ultimately act for Han and not for Qin. This is simply human nature. The King of Qin agreed with their view and handed Fei over to the judicial officials for trial. Li Si sent a messenger to deliver poison to Fei, instructing him to commit suicide. Establishing exaltation as the ultimate peak, no one in the world can add to or subtract from it. The root and branch accord with each other.

Great rites share moderation with Heaven and Earth.

<margin><term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Jijie commentary</gloss>: Zheng Xuan says: This means according with the vital breath of Heaven and Earth and their numerical measures.</margin>

<margin><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: This means that Heaven has the sun and moon, and Earth has mountains and rivers. High and low have distinct forms, and their generative functions are each different. Great rites distinguish nobility and baseness, honor and humility, marking their gradations and differences: this is how great rites share moderation with Heaven and Earth.</margin>

Because of harmony, the hundred things do not lose their course.

<margin><term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Jijie commentary</gloss>: Zheng Xuan says: They do not lose their innate nature.</margin>

<margin><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: Music shares harmony with Heaven and Earth, and is able to generate and fulfill the innate nature of the ten thousand things.</margin>

Because of moderation, sacrifices are offered to Heaven and Earth.

<margin><term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Jijie commentary</gloss>: For their merit in completing things, recompense is offered to them.</margin>

<margin><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: Rites share moderation with Heaven and Earth. With nobility and baseness, superior and inferior clearly ordered, one offers recompense for the merit of generating and completing the ten thousand things.</margin>

In the manifest realm, there are rites and music.

<margin><term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Jijie commentary</gloss>: These are what teach people.</margin>

<margin><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: "Manifest" is like "external". It means that the sage king can cause music to harmonize with Heaven and Earth, and rites to share moderation with Heaven and Earth, and can make these rites and music luminous to instruct the people.</margin>

In the hidden realm, there are ghosts and spirits.

<margin><term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Jijie commentary</gloss>: Zheng Xuan says: They assist Heaven and Earth in completing things. The Book of Changes says: "One understands the conditions and circumstances of ghosts and spirits." In that case, the refined vital breath of a sage is called a spirit, and the refined vital breath of a worthy or wise person is called a ghost.</margin>

<margin><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: "Hidden" means internal. It means that the sage king can inwardly revere ghosts and spirits, assisting Heaven and Earth to generate and complete the ten thousand things.</margin>

When matters are like this, within the Four Seas, all join in reverence and unite in love.

<summary>This passage expounds on the cosmological foundations of music and rites, showing how great music accords with cosmic harmony to nourish all creatures, while great rites mirror cosmic distinctions and moderation. It explains the dual operation of rites and music in the visible realm to educate humankind, alongside reverence for spirits in the hidden realm, thereby cultivating universal respect and love across the empire.</summary>

Receiving the imperial decree, we hurried forward like mallards skimming the water; joining the distinguished ranks of the court, we rejoiced like leaping sparrows. Fine editions have been bestowed from the imperial library <note>original: "秘閣" (*Mi Ge*)</note>, where jade-like volumes assemble in profusion; our duty offices stand close to the forbidden palace grounds, adjacent to the crystalline halls of the celestial realm <note>original: "蕊珠之館" (*Ruizhu zhi Guan*), poetically evoking the imperial library pavilions</note>. Burning the midnight oil, the evening collation continues as the moon already peeks through the blinds; grinding ink for early-morning writing, the dawn breeze turns the manuscript leaves. Rejoicing in this grand occasion of the literary world, we completely forget the toil of our usual labors. Yet the critical verification of these various histories presents difficulties far more intense than comparing variations among the Confucian Classics. The concluding records of an earlier history form the very starting point of the subsequent history; the intertwined events of the southern dynasties are likewise stitched together in the northern histories. As each author wrote according to their own perspective, divergences naturally arose, producing confusion and error. How could there be no sound reading among them? Yet extracting excerpts easily breeds tedious redundancy.

fathers became righteous, mothers loving, elder brothers friendly, younger brothers respectful, and sons filial. Within, there was peace; without, accomplishment was achieved.

<note>Correct Meaning: Du Yu says: "Within" refers to the various Xia states, and "without" refers to the Yi and Di border peoples. In our view, Xie established the teachings of the Five Constants, so that the Xia realms enjoyed great peace and the outer peoples turned toward civilization.</note>

In ancient times, the lineage of Dihong had an unworthy son,

<note>Collected Explanations: Jia Kui says Dihong refers to the Yellow Emperor. The unworthy son was his descendant, Huandou.</note>

who suppressed righteousness, concealed wickedness, and took pleasure in committing evil deeds. All under Heaven called him Hundun <gloss>Chaos</gloss>.

<note>Correct Meaning: "Te" </note><note>original: "慝"</note> means evil. Another edition states: "The people of all under Heaven called him Hundun." Hundun was Huandou. This means he suppressed righteous deeds, secretly worked harm, and delighted in vicious malice, which is why he was called Hundun. Du Yu says that Hundun describes an appearance of being closed and unenlightened. The Classic of Divine Marvels <note>original: "神異經"</note> states: "West of the Kunlun mountains there is a beast. Its form resembles a dog with long fur and four feet like a brown bear but without claws. It has eyes but cannot see, and its steps do not advance. It has two ears but cannot hear, yet it senses when human beings pass. It has a belly without five internal organs, and its neck is straight and short so food passes straight through. When it encounters someone of virtuous conduct, it charges and butts them. When it encounters someone who acts with malice and wickedness, it leans upon and relies on them. Its name is Hundun." Furthermore, Zhuangzi says: "The Emperor of the Southern Sea was Shu <gloss>Brief</gloss>, the Emperor of the Northern Sea was Hu <gloss>Sudden</gloss>, and the Emperor of the Center was Hundun <gloss>Chaos</gloss>.
